name: Wipers
label: Park Avenue
lede: Greg Sage's four-track punk from Portland went nowhere for a decade, then Kurt Cobain started saying it was where Nirvana learned everything.

eras.title: A window washer with a four-track
eras.text: Greg Sage was cutting records at home as a kid and playing blues-rock for a pro wrestler before punk existed. By 1978 he had a band, a rehearsal room and his own label, and he wanted his records to sound like clean glass.

years.src: Far Out: Wipers and wrestlers · Wikipedia: Greg Sage
years.h: Sage cuts a blues-rock LP for a pro wrestler
years.p: Portland wrestler Beauregarde hired teenage guitarist [[Greg Sage|275a4de2-cdc4-445b-b17a-501b0f75e460]] and bassist Dave Koupal to record his album in a single afternoon.
years.xp:
Sage first saw Beauregarde (born Larry Pitchford) on Portland Wrestling television in 1969. Far Out reports the wrestler approached him at a show where Sage was filling in on guitar, and the LP came out in 1971 on F-Empire.

Sage told Far Out that the studio engineer grabbed him by the collar and dragged him to the office to show off his framed certificates, and Beauregarde had the engineer replaced. Sage reissued the record years later through his own Zeno label.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band) · Wikipedia: Greg Sage · Rolling Stone: Wipers' Is This Real? at 40
years.h: The Wipers form in Portland, named after a window-cleaning job
years.p: Sage, drummer Sam Henry and bassist Dave Koupal start the band. Wikipedia says the name came from Sage cleaning windows at a movie theater and wanting his music that transparent.
years.xp: Sources disagree on the start year: Wikipedia has 1977, Rolling Stone says 1978. Either way, the trio was one of the first punk bands in the Pacific Northwest.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band) · Wikipedia: Greg Sage
years.h: "Better Off Dead": 45 on Sage's own Trap label
years.p: The first Wipers single was recorded on Sage's 4-track in the band's rehearsal space and put out on Trap, the label he ran himself.
years.xp: Trap grew into Portland's punk imprint, putting out singles by the Stiphnoyds, the Neo Boys and Sado Nation, and the 1979 live comp 10-29-79. Wikipedia dates the label to 1979 in Sage's biography but lists the 1978 single as a Trap release.

q: Everything had to be a compromise.
years.src: Rolling Stone: Wipers' Is This Real? at 40 · Wikipedia: Is This Real?
years.h: Sage wanted a 4-track LP. The label wanted a real studio.
years.p: Is This Real? gets recorded at Recording Associates in Portland after Sage is told his home tapes won't do.
years.xp:
Sage had planned to make the album on his 4-track in the rehearsal room. He told Rolling Stone that once he was pushed into a proper studio, he realized everything from then on would be a compromise.

He kept control anyway: he produced the record and split it into a Pos side and a Neg side rather than an A and a B.

eras.title: Pos, Neg, and a ten-minute song
eras.text: Three records in four years, two new rhythm sections, and a sound that got heavier and stranger each time. Almost nobody outside the Northwest was buying, but Europe was listening.

years.src: Wikipedia: Is This Real? · BrooklynVegan: 15 songs that influenced Nirvana (probably)
yt: Return of the Rat, from Is This Real?
years.h: Is This Real? on Park Avenue
years.p: The debut LP got little promotion and a small local following, and the opening riff of "Return of the Rat" outlasted everything around it.
years.xp:
Robert Christgau praised Sage's "hard-edged vocals" and "economical one-hook construction." AllMusic later allowed that the drums sound tinny and the songs win anyway.

BrooklynVegan points to "Potential Suicide" as the song Nirvana turned into the riff of "Breed."

years.src: Wikipedia: Alien Boy
years.h: Alien Boy EP: a song about a friend, and three outtakes
years.p: The title track went on side A. Side B held "Image of Man," "Telepathic Love" and "Voices in the Rain," leftovers from the Is This Real? sessions.
years.xp: Sage said the song came from his friend James "Jim Jim" Chasse, whose conversations and sense of vision fed several songs on the LP. The EP runs 8 minutes 54 seconds.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Henry joins the Rats, Koupal moves to Ohio, two Brads step in
years.p: Drummer Brad Naish (ex-Stiphnoyds) and bassist Brad Davidson replace the original rhythm section.
years.xp: Sam Henry went on to Napalm Beach, formed in 1982 with Chris Newman, and stayed in the Portland scene for the rest of his life.

years.src: Wikipedia: Youth of America · The Quietus: 30 Years On, The Wipers' Youth Of America Revisited
years.h: Youth of America: six songs, one of them ten and a half minutes
years.p: Recorded at Wave Sound in Vancouver, Washington, in the middle of hardcore's two-minute era. It did better in Europe than at home.
years.xp:
The title track runs 10:30 and "When It's Over" 6:30 on a 30-minute LP. The Quietus called it searching, unromantic punk that borrowed from motorik Krautrock and goth.

Pitchfork later put the album at No. 102 on its list of the 200 best albums of the 1980s, and the title track at No. 173 among the songs. Melvins and Mission of Burma covered it.

years.src: Wikipedia: Over the Edge (Wipers album) · Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Over the Edge: shorter songs, and the first radio play
years.p: The third LP tightened up after Youth of America and brought the band its first real modern-rock airplay.
years.xp:
A different take of "Romeo" had come out as a Trap single in 1982, with "No Solution" on the B-side. Hole covered the title track, and so did Red Fang and Mono Men.

J Mascis of Dinosaur Jr. has named Sage's guitar playing on this record as a foundation for his own.

years.src: Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost · Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Brain Eater folds without paying the band
years.p: The label that released Over the Edge went under, and Rock and Roll Globe reports Sage was left unpaid.
years.xp: Wikipedia says a label bankruptcy left Sage financially stranded and that he recorded his solo album Straight Ahead for Enigma to recover. It names Park Avenue Records; Rock and Roll Globe names Brain Eater.

eras.title: Sage builds a room called 421
eras.text: After the label wreckage, Sage took control: his own studio, his own tapes, a five-album deal with Restless. The Wipers became a trio built around Steve Plouf, and the records got heavier and more finished.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band) · Razorcake: Interview with Greg Sage
years.h: Sage goes solo on Enigma and produces Beat Happening
years.p: Enigma also pressed the live Wipers Tour 84 on vinyl. Straight Ahead came out under his name, and he produced the self-titled debut by Olympia's [[Beat Happening|449e44cb-bcae-4c48-a1af-5d8df0f81456]] in an old fire station.

years.src: Wikipedia: Land of the Lost (Wipers album) · Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost
years.h: Land of the Lost: Restless signs the band, Plouf sits down at the kit
years.p: Recorded at Sage's own 421 Sound in Portland with [[Brad Davidson|62979f1a-3e6c-4865-b775-d176f6119628]] on bass and Steve Plouf on drums, the first of three Restless albums made there. "Let Me Know" later appeared on the River's Edge soundtrack (Enigma, 1987).
years.xp:
Maximum Rocknroll called the title track heavier and riffier than anything the Wipers had tried. Rock and Roll Globe says Restless gave the band a stable six-year deal for five albums, and Plouf stayed in the band 13 years.

The Spin Alternative Record Guide called it the most definitive Wipers record for sound and songwriting.

years.src: Rolling Stone: Wipers' Is This Real? at 40 · Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Follow Blind, the one Sage says he likes best
years.p: Rolling Stone reports it is his favorite of his own records, made at 421 Sound between the Restless albums.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: The Circle: the last Restless album
years.p: The final record of the Portland run, cut at 421 Sound.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band) · Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost
yt: Greg Sage interview, VPRO radio, 29 March 1989
years.h: Sage calls it: no studio, no money, no more Wipers
years.p: A tour with drummer Travis McNabb ends the band. Davidson moves to London and Sage to Phoenix.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says Sage ended the band over frustration with the music industry and the loss of his studio space. Dutch radio (VPRO) interviewed him on 29 March 1989, during the final stretch.

Rock and Roll Globe quotes Sage's own goal for the group: 15 albums in 10 years.

eras.title: Kurt keeps naming names
eras.text: With the band gone, Nirvana turned the Wipers into required reading. Kurt Cobain said it in fanzines, on the BBC and on a tribute box set.

q: We learnt everything from the Wipers.
years.src: Rolling Stone Australia: Return of the Rat · Rolling Stone: Wipers' Is This Real? at 40 · Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost
years.h: Kurt Cobain tells an English fanzine what Nirvana owes Portland
years.p: Speaking to a British fanzine, [[Kurt Cobain|3c9b356d-d1db-4f4e-a7a3-2d00c1d70255]] said Nirvana learned everything from the Wipers, a punk and hard-rock mix at a time when nobody cared.
years.xp:
Cobain also called the Wipers the most innovative punk rock band, about 15 years too early, according to the Rolling Stone feature.

Rock and Roll Globe adds that Cobain went to Wipers shows as a kid.

years.src: Live Nirvana: 10/21/90 Maida Vale Studios · Rolling Stone Australia: Return of the Rat · Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: [[Nirvana|5b11f4ce-a62d-471e-81fc-a69a8278c7da]] cut "D-7" for John Peel at Maida Vale
years.p: The Wipers cover was recorded for Peel's BBC session and later surfaced on the Hormoaning EP and as a B-side to the UK "Lithium" CD single.

years.src: Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost
years.h: Cobain offers Sage the whole Nevermind tour. He plays one show.
years.p: Rock and Roll Globe reports the invitation covered the entire tour and that Sage took only a single Los Angeles date.

years.src: Rolling Stone Australia: Return of the Rat · Wikipedia: Eight Songs for Greg Sage and the Wipers
years.h: Nirvana records "Return of the Rat" in one or two takes
years.p: Cobain's reported answer when Geffen blocked "D-7" for the tribute. It was cut at Laundry Room Studio in West Seattle with Barrett Jones.
years.xp:
Thor Lindsay, who founded the label behind Eight Songs for Greg Sage and the Wipers, is the source for the quote. Cobain then sent the new track in on DAT.

Rolling Stone Australia says the band had never played "Return of the Rat" before that session.

years.src: Wikipedia: Eight Songs for Greg Sage and the Wipers · Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Eight Songs for Greg Sage and the Wipers box set
years.p: Tim/Kerr issued four colored 7-inches in a run of 10,000 with Nirvana, [[Hole|1dcc8968-f2cd-441c-beda-6270f70f2863]], [[Poison Idea|86871dd7-f50c-40bb-a298-a144775b64ae]] and Napalm Beach.
years.xp: Hole took "Over the Edge," Poison Idea "Up Front" and Napalm Beach "Potential Suicide." The expanded CD, Fourteen Songs, added [[Nation of Ulysses|ae888df0-2a19-4895-a654-e0093875d5b6]] and [[Thurston Moore|8ba48525-d922-42ee-9775-97b7b8f9712e]].

eras.title: Two men, one studio
eras.text: Sage reformed the Wipers as a duo with Plouf, moved the operation to Phoenix and kept making records on his own terms, on Tim/Kerr and then his own Zeno label.

years.src: Wikipedia: Is This Real? · Wikipedia: Alien Boy
years.h: Sub Pop reissues Is This Real? on CD with the Alien Boy tracks
years.p: Sub Pop added the EP's tracks to the remaster and used the cover art from the 1987 German pressing.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Silver Sail: Sage and Plouf as a duo
years.p: Tim/Kerr put out the album that restarted the band.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: The Herd
years.p: Second Tim/Kerr album of the duo years. "Return of the Rat" also appeared that year on the Hype! soundtrack from Sub Pop.

years.src: Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost
years.h: Last known Wipers show: New Music Seminar, New York
years.p: Rock and Roll Globe lists it as the band's final concert.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band) · Rolling Stone: Wipers' Is This Real? at 40
years.h: Power in One on Sage's own Zeno label
years.p: The last Wipers album, and the first on the label Sage founded himself.
years.xp: Rolling Stone reports Sage put out nine more records after the debut and stepped away from public view after 1999.

eras.title: Everybody else catches up
eras.text: The records stayed out of print, the covers kept coming, and a documentary named after a Wipers song. Sage kept running Zeno from Phoenix.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band) · BrooklynVegan: 15 songs that influenced Nirvana (probably)
years.h: Cloud Nothings' Dylan Baldi: "I was basically trying to be the Wipers"
years.p: [[J Mascis|82315599-2215-4c3e-a36f-87be58d06ec0]], [[Mudhoney|e675295a-1efe-4247-aa3b-53b78d0cdffc]], Hot Snakes and Metz also cite them, and Cobain's journals list the first three Wipers albums among his top 50.

years.src: Wikipedia: James Chasse · Wikipedia: Alien Boy
years.h: James Chasse dies in Portland police custody
years.p: The Multnomah County medical examiner ruled the death accidental, from blunt force trauma.
years.xp: Chasse was the friend behind "Alien Boy." Brian Lindstrom's documentary Alien Boy: The Life and Death of James Chasse premiered in Portland on February 15, 2013, and takes its name from the Wipers song.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Sam Henry, original drummer, dies at 65
years.p: Wikipedia gives complications of stomach cancer.
